name: Memory T cell
markers: CD45RO (human marker; naive T cells carry CD45RA instead)
CCR7 and CD62L (central memory cells only)
CD103 (integrin αE; epidermal resident CD8 memory cells)
CLA (cutaneous lymphocyte antigen; human skin-homing marker)
summary: A T cell that met its antigen before and survived after the infection cleared, so it responds faster and more strongly the second time. Some circulate between blood and lymph nodes; others settle in tissues such as skin, where they act as local guards. One record covers both CD4 and CD8 memory cells.
functions: Arises when a few of the naive CD4 or CD8 T cells that answered an infection survive it (around 5-10% of killer CD8 T cells). Their numbers are then kept up for years by IL-7 and IL-15, without antigen.

Debated: where memory cells come from. Some may be effector cells that survive and change, others may branch off earlier in the response; the evidence differs between experiments and between CD4 and CD8 cells.

Responds faster and more strongly on a second meeting: a memory cell needs less co-stimulation than a naive cell, divides sooner and makes effector cytokines such as IFN-γ and TNF within hours. Memory CD8 cells kill infected cells on sight; memory CD4 cells help B cells and macrophages and make the cytokines of the helper type they came from.

Comes in three main kinds. Central memory cells (CCR7 and CD62L positive) circulate through blood and lymph nodes and divide readily when re-challenged. Effector memory cells (CCR7 negative) patrol blood and tissues and act at once. Resident memory cells (CD69 positive) stay in one tissue and do not recirculate.

Goes to skin when primed there. Memory T cells with the skin-homing marker CLA, which binds E-selectin on dermal vessels, also carry the chemokine receptors CCR4 and CCR10, which respond to chemokines made in skin, such as CCL17 and CCL27 (the latter made by epidermal keratinocytes).

Skin holds a huge store. An adult's skin contains about 2 × 10¹⁰ T cells, nearly twice the number in the circulation, and most CLA-positive effector memory T cells are estimated to be resident in skin at rest.

Settles in the skin as resident memory cells. In mice, after vaccinia virus infection of the skin, CD8 resident memory cells fill the whole skin, do not recirculate and protect it better than circulating central memory cells. Their formation in the epidermis needs IL-15 and TGF-β. In people, most skin resident memory cells are CD4 and sit in the dermis (unlike mice), while CD103-positive CD4 and CD8 cells sit in the epidermis; CD8 cells with CD49a make IFN-γ and can kill, whereas CD49a-negative CD8 cells make IL-17.

Sounds the alarm when it meets antigen again. In mice, reactivated resident memory CD8 cells switched on antiviral and antibacterial genes across the skin around them, protecting against an unrelated virus, and, in the female reproductive tract, made dendritic cells mature and activated NK cells.

Rests in the bone marrow. In mice, most memory CD4 T cells move to the marrow within weeks of an immune response and sit beside IL-7-making stromal cells, resting but quick to respond. Human marrow memory CD4 T cells are also resting and hold much of the memory for systemic infections such as measles.

Debated: how permanent residency is. Resident memory cells were thought never to leave tissue, but reactivated resident cells in mouse gut rejoined the circulation, and memory cells from skin and mucosa gave rise to resident memory cells in the draining lymph nodes.
abundance: Rare in newborns and accumulate through life with infections. Most of the body's memory T cells are in tissues and lymphoid organs rather than blood. Laboratory mice, kept very clean, have far fewer memory T cells than adult people, like newborn humans; mice living in barns or with pet-shop mice gain human-like memory populations.
